name: Calcium hydroxylapatite filler (Radiesse)

card.summary: A dense, collagen-stimulating injectable filler used for cheeks, jawline and chin definition; reasonably studied for ageing faces, with little trial data on young-adult 'bony' looksmaxxing goals.
card.aka: CaHA, Radiesse, high G prime filler
card.note: Not reversible with hyaluronidase; nodules are the most commonly reported adverse event, and vascular complications are a documented risk of all fillers.

quick.overview:
Calcium hydroxylapatite (CaHA) filler, best known under the brand name Radiesse, consists of tiny calcium-based microspheres suspended in a gel. It is injected by clinicians to add volume and structure to areas such as the cheeks, jawline and chin, and is also reported to stimulate the body's own collagen.

In looksmaxxing communities it is discussed as a stiffer, 'high G prime' alternative to hyaluronic acid filler for creating a more defined, bone-like jaw and chin without surgery. Published research mostly concerns ageing patients rather than young people seeking contour.
quick.mechanism: The gel carrier provides immediate volume, while the microspheres act as a scaffold that, according to reviews, prompts nearby cells to produce collagen, elastin and other tissue components. The gel is gradually absorbed over time, and the effect that remains is attributed to this newly formed tissue.
quick.risks: A review of 21 studies covering 5,081 treatments reported adverse events in about 3 percent of treatments, most of them nodules. Fillers as a category carry a rare but serious risk of vascular occlusion, including blindness. In the US, Radiesse is a prescription-only medical device used by licensed providers; its approved indications are limited and jawline or chin use is off-label in many markets.

lead: Calcium hydroxylapatite filler, sold most prominently as Radiesse (Merz Aesthetics), is an injectable soft-tissue filler made of calcium hydroxylapatite microspheres suspended in a carboxymethylcellulose gel [3][1]. It is classed as a biostimulatory filler because, besides giving immediate volume, it is reported to induce new collagen, elastin and blood vessel formation in the tissue around it [3].

Clinicians use it for wrinkles and folds, cheek and jawline contouring, facial lipoatrophy in people with HIV, and hand rejuvenation; off-label uses include skin-tightening with diluted or hyperdiluted preparations [2][1]. In looksmaxxing communities it is discussed under the label 'high G prime filler', as a firmer non-surgical option for adding structure to the jaw, chin and cheekbones.

A 2024 systematic review concluded that CaHA/CMC may be considered a safe and effective option for the cheeks, jawline, HIV-related lipoatrophy and nasolabial folds, but also noted that no randomized controlled trials had been published on the newer diluted and hyperdiluted techniques [2]. A review of safety literature found nodules to be by far the most commonly reported adverse event [4].

paras: Radiesse is made of calcium hydroxylapatite microspheres suspended in a carboxymethylcellulose gel. The gel gives an immediate effect and is gradually absorbed, while the microspheres remain and act as a cell scaffold [3]. Calcium hydroxylapatite is also the mineral form found in bone and teeth, which is the reason some forum users associate it with a 'bone-like' result.

The material has been characterised as having strong rheological properties, a feature reviewers link to its versatility in volumizing and contouring areas that need lift [2]. A laboratory comparison of calcium hydroxylapatite and hyaluronic acid fillers measured differences in viscosity and elasticity between the two categories to help clinicians choose a filler for volume replacement [E4 not cited here].

On-label uses of CaHA/CMC include filling wrinkles and lines, volumizing and contouring; reviewers also describe off-label uses aimed at biostimulation and skin tightening [2]. On the body, the only FDA-approved indication reported in a 2024 review is treatment of the hands, with a European Union approval for the decolletage [1].

Systematic review data suggest CaHA/CMC responds well in the cheeks and jawline, and that marionette lines, chin, pre-jowl area and the corners of the mouth also tend to respond with a high degree of efficacy [2]. A review of lower-face reshaping describes the jawline and chin as central to a youthful or sexually dimorphic facial appearance and discusses fillers as a means of redefining the mandibular angle and line [5].

In looksmaxxing forums, users describe CaHA as a 'structural' filler used to create sharper jaw and chin contours, usually compared with hyaluronic acid products of differing stiffness. Much of the published literature concerns ageing patients; no published trials were identified that were designed around young adults pursuing facial definition.

CaHA/CMC has been used for HIV-related facial lipoatrophy [2], hand volume loss [6], and, in related formulations, for injection augmentation of the vocal folds [E7 not cited here]. Registered trials have also examined CaHA for cellulite dimples in the buttocks and for gum recession and tooth hypersensitivity, according to ClinicalTrials.gov [ct4][ct1].

Evidence for facial use is largely drawn from observational studies, case series and comparative histology studies, with systematic reviews rating CaHA/CMC as effective for cheeks, jawline and nasolabial folds [2]. For body treatment and for diluted or hyperdiluted products, reviewers state that recent trends and guidelines have yet to be supported by randomized controlled trials, despite a good safety profile in clinical practice [1][2].

A multicenter randomized trial has examined the long-term duration and safety of a lidocaine-containing version of Radiesse for the jawline [11]. A randomized split-face study in 24 women aged 35 to 45 compared biopsies after Radiesse with those after a hyaluronic acid filler to assess collagen and elastin production [8]. A separate randomized comparison of gene expression after poly-L-lactic acid and CaHA injection reported that the two biostimulators act through different pathways, with the report's title describing CaHA as inducing an inflammatory response [7].

A review of 21 peer-reviewed articles covering 5,081 treatments in 2,779 patients found 173 adverse events (3 percent). Of those, 96 percent were nodules; the rest were persistent inflammation or swelling, persistent redness and overcorrection. About half the nodules occurred in dynamic areas, and in most cases the nodules were not visible and resolved without intervention [4].

As with other dermal fillers, accidental injection into or compression of blood vessels can cause tissue necrosis or vision loss; a review of cases of blindness after cosmetic filler injection describes the complication as rare but feared, and mostly irreversible [E2 not cited here]. Wikipedia's overview of dermal fillers lists bruising, redness and pain as common effects and retrograde embolization causing blindness as rare but serious [w1].

Published human studies include systematic reviews of facial and body use [2][1], a safety review of 21 studies [4], randomized split-face and multicenter trials comparing CaHA with hyaluronic acid or poly-L-lactic acid, or assessing the jawline [8][7][11], and a prospective trial of chest rejuvenation [12]. A pilot study examined diluted CaHA in the neck and decolletage [E9 not cited here].

Registered trials on ClinicalTrials.gov include a study of cheek flattening (NCT01225354), a Phase 4 trial of restoring facial volume after GLP-1 weight loss (NCT07419854), and a pivotal-style study for nasolabial folds (NCT07856797) [ct5][ct3][ct10]. None of these registered trials is specifically about young adults seeking facial definition for aesthetic ideals.

On looksmax.org, discussion of hydroxyapatite more often concerns solid facial implants than the injectable Radiesse; one thread starter describes hydroxyapatite implants as the closest material to real bone and says they should be discussed more, while a reply argues that implant material barely matters [l1]. Injectable CaHA is generally described by forum users as a way to trial a firmer jaw or chin look before surgery, though these are user opinions rather than research findings.

lore.intro: Community discussion treats CaHA as the 'structure' filler in a toolkit that also includes softer hyaluronic acid products, and sometimes conflates it with hydroxyapatite bone implants [l1].

claims.claim: High G prime filler can mimic bone and sharpen the jaw or chin without surgery.
claims.believers: Forum users say stiffer fillers add structure where bone is perceived as deficient and can serve as a trial before implants or osteotomy [l1].
claims.experts: Reviews describe CaHA/CMC as effective for cheeks, jawline and chin in ageing and volume-depleted patients, but these studies do not address young adults seeking a skeletal ideal [2][5].

claims.claim: Hydroxyapatite implants are the closest thing to real bone and deserve more attention.
claims.believers: One looksmax.org thread starter argues hydroxyapatite is the nearest material to bone and cites before-and-after photos from one surgeon [l1].
claims.experts: No published comparative trial in the supplied literature compares hydroxyapatite facial implants with silicone, PEEK or Medpor implants; respondents in the thread themselves question whether implant material matters [l1].
